draft.title: Mean, median, mode and range
card: Mean
Add all the values, then divide by how many values there are.
Median
Put the values in order. The median is the middle one. If there are two middle values, find the number halfway between them.
Mode
The value that appears most often.
Range
Highest value minus lowest value. Example: for 3, 5, 5, 6, 11 the mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6, the median is 5, the mode is 5 and the range is 11 − 3 = 8.
draft.remember: Mean shares the total out evenly. Median is the middle. Mode is the most common. Range is the spread.

a.q: Sam scored 4, 7, 7, 9 and 13 in five quizzes. What is the mean score?
a.why: The total is 4 + 7 + 7 + 9 + 13 = 40, and 40 ÷ 5 = 8. The answer 7 is the median and the mode, not the mean.
a.clue: Add all five scores, then divide by 5.

b.q: Jess counted the pencils in six pencil cases: 12, 5, 9, 5, 14, 9. What is the median number of pencils?
b.why: In order the values are 5, 5, 9, 9, 12, 14. The two middle values are both 9, so the median is 9. The answer 5 is tempting but is the lowest value, and 8 would be the mean, not the median.
b.clue: Put the values in order first, then find the middle two.

problems.detail: The why says 8 would be the mean, but the mean is 54 ÷ 6 = 9, not 8. None of the options is the mean worked out wrongly as 8 here, so this explanation teaches a false calculation.

The mean of this data set is also 9, the same as the median, so a student who mixes up mean and median still gets the right answer. The two middle values are also equal, so the halfway rule from the card is never really tested. A data set with a mean that differs from the median, and two different middle values, would test the idea properly.

check.summary: The card and question a are correct. Question b's explanation wrongly says the mean is 8, when it is 9 and equal to the median, so the question cannot tell mean from median and should use different data.
